lessons.title: Commercial Risks: Vacancy, Tenant Concentration and Obsolescence

children.text: In the 1990s, Nariman Point was where every serious company in Mumbai wanted an office. Over the following two decades, banks, consultancies and multinationals steadily moved to Bandra Kurla Complex, with its newer buildings, larger floor plates and shorter commutes from the suburbs. Nobody's tenant defaulted in a single dramatic moment. Owners in older buildings simply found that each lease renewal brought lower rents, longer vacancies and fewer interested tenants. That slow slide is what commercial risk usually looks like: rare, quiet, and very expensive when it arrives.

body.text: Commercial property pays more than residential because its risks come in large, lumpy doses. One empty unit, one dominant tenant or one ageing building can erase years of higher yield.

children.text: Risk 1: Vacancy, and What It Really Costs

Residential vacancy means a month or two without rent. Commercial vacancy is a different animal. Business tenants take months to decide, need approvals from head offices, and expect a rent-free period to fit out. Meanwhile, you keep paying the costs the tenant used to cover. The true cost of a tenant leaving is much more than the empty months.

body.latex: \text{Cost of Tenant Exit} = \text{Lost Rent} + \text{Holding Costs} + \text{New Rent-Free Period} + \text{Brokerage} + \text{Refurbishment}

children.text: Take a Gurugram office unit renting at ₹3 lakh a month. The tenant leaves at the end of its lease. It takes 9 months to find a new one, who asks for 3 rent-free months. Here is the bill.

children.text: One tenant change cost 16 months of rent. On a unit yielding 7.5% gross, that single event wipes out well over a year of income. Across India, office vacancy has hovered in the mid-teens percent in recent years, with huge gaps between strong and weak micro-markets and between new and old buildings, so vacancy is not a remote possibility.
Risk 2: Tenant Concentration

A single-tenant unit is a binary bet. While the tenant pays, you earn the full rent. When it leaves, you earn nothing. A building with many tenants absorbs one exit and keeps most of its income. This is why REITs with hundreds of tenants can report steady distributions while an individual owner of one unit lives through feast and famine.

body.title: Rent still coming in after one equal-sized tenant leaves (% of original)

children.text: Concentration also hides in less obvious places. Owning three office units in the same building is still one building's risk. Owning shops leased entirely to fashion retailers is one sector's risk. Owning offices all let to IT services firms exposes you to one industry's hiring cycle. Diversification in commercial property means spreading across tenants, sectors, buildings and locations, which is hard to achieve with a few crore rupees in direct property.

body.text: This is the strongest case for REITs for individual investors. A single REIT unit gives you a slice of many buildings, hundreds of tenants and several cities, something a direct buyer with ₹2 crore can never replicate.

children.text: Risk 3: Obsolescence

markDefs.definition: When a building no longer meets what tenants need, such as small floor plates, low ceilings, weak power supply, poor air handling or no green certification, even if it is structurally sound.
When the area around a building loses its appeal to tenants, often because business activity moves to a newer district with better buildings, transport or amenities.

children.text: Buildings age in two ways.
Functional obsolescence

is when the building itself falls behind: small floor plates, low ceilings, inadequate power backup, poor air handling, too little parking, or no green certification such as LEED or IGBC, which many multinational tenants now expect.
Locational obsolescence
is when the neighbourhood falls behind, as business activity shifts to newer districts.

columns.label: Functional
points: Fixable with capital spending, if the owners agree

columns.label: Locational
points: Business activity moves to a newer district
Metro or expressway changes commuting patterns
Newer supply nearby undercuts on rent

markDefs.definition: A trend where tenants move from older or lower-grade buildings to newer, better-specified ones, often at similar rents, leaving older stock with rising vacancy.

children.text: The result is a
flight to quality

. When new Grade A supply arrives at competitive rents, tenants upgrade and older buildings are left with rising vacancy and falling rents. The same pattern applies to warehouses, where modern tenants need high clear heights and proper truck docks, and to malls competing with better-run centres and online shopping.

body.text: Strata buildings suffer most from obsolescence. Upgrading lifts, air-conditioning or facades needs agreement and money from dozens of owners, which rarely happens. A single-owner building can refurbish and reposition itself. A strata building often just ages.

children.text: Risk 4: Rising Cap Rates

Even with the same tenant paying the same rent, the value of your property can fall. When interest rates rise or investors become more cautious, buyers demand a higher cap rate, and value drops mechanically.

body.label: Cap rate expansion
body.context: A property earning ₹30 lakh of net operating income is worth ₹4 crore at a 7.5% cap rate but about ₹3.53 crore at 8.5%, with no change in rent.

children.text: Early Warning Signs and How to Respond

cells: Rising "To Let" boards in the building, longer leasing times nearby
Keep a cash reserve of 12 to 18 months of rent; renew tenants early
Late payments, layoffs, requests to cut space or rent
Strong deposits, tenant credit checks, diversify tenants
One tenant, one sector or one building dominates your income
Spread across assets or use REITs for part of the allocation
Tenants citing poor power, cooling, parking or no green certification
Plan capital spending; avoid ageing strata buildings
Major employers relocating, new districts drawing tenants
Favour locations with transport links and sustained employer demand
Rising interest rates, falling REIT prices
Avoid overpaying at very low cap rates; borrow conservatively

body.title: Calculate: The Cost of an Exit in Bengaluru
body.prompt: A Bengaluru office unit rents for ₹2 lakh a month. The tenant leaves, and the unit sits vacant for 6 months, with the owner paying CAM of ₹20,000 a month. The new tenant gets 2 rent-free months, and brokerage is 1.5 months' rent. Ignoring other costs, what is the total cost of the exit, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Lost rent: 6 × ₹2 lakh = ₹12 lakh. CAM: 6 × ₹0.2 lakh = ₹1.2 lakh. Rent-free: 2 × ₹2 lakh = ₹4 lakh. Brokerage: 1.5 × ₹2 lakh = ₹3 lakh. Total: ₹20.2 lakh, or about 10 months of rent.

body.title: Quick Check: Value Without a Vacancy
body.question: A fully leased office earns ₹40 lakh of net operating income. Interest rates rise and buyers now demand a 9% cap rate instead of 8%. Rent is unchanged. What happens to value?
options: It stays at ₹5 crore because rent has not changed
It falls from ₹5 crore to about ₹4.44 crore
It rises to ₹5.5 crore because rates are higher
body.explanation: At 8%: ₹40 lakh ÷ 0.08 = ₹5 crore. At 9%: ₹40 lakh ÷ 0.09 = about ₹4.44 crore. A one percentage point rise in cap rate cuts value by about 11% with no change in income.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Tenants Upgrading
body.textWithBlank: When tenants leave older buildings for newer, better-specified ones at similar rents, the trend is called a flight to ___.
body.explanation: A flight to quality leaves older and lower-grade buildings with rising vacancy, especially when new Grade A supply is available nearby.

body.title: Scenario: Three Units, One Building
body.scenario: Vikram owns three strata office units, each about 1,500 sq ft, on different floors of an 18-year-old building in Noida Sector 62. All three are leased to small IT services firms, together providing ₹4.5 lakh a month, most of his retirement income. One tenant has given notice after cutting staff. Two new Grade A buildings with green certification have opened a few kilometres away at similar rents. The building's owners' association has been unable to agree on replacing its old air-conditioning plant.
body.prompt: What risks is Vikram exposed to, and what should he do?
body.modelAnswer: He faces all three major commercial risks at once. Vacancy: one exit could cost him many months of rent on that unit once lost rent, CAM, brokerage and a rent-free period are counted. Concentration: all three units are in one building, in one micro-market, let to tenants in one sector, so an IT slowdown hits all his income together. Obsolescence: the building is ageing, the owners cannot agree on upgrades, and new Grade A supply nearby offers tenants a better product at similar rents, a textbook flight to quality. He should build a cash reserve immediately, offer the departing tenant's space at a realistic rent with flexible terms to shorten vacancy, and approach his other two tenants early about renewals. Over the next few years he should seriously consider selling one or two units while they are still leased, since leased units sell far better than empty ones, and redeploying part of the money into assets that diversify his income, such as REITs.

cards.definition: Lost rent plus holding costs, rent-free period, brokerage and refurbishment when a tenant leaves.
Dependence on one or a few tenants, sectors or buildings for most of your rental income.
A building falling behind tenant needs, such as floor plates, power, cooling or green certification.
A neighbourhood losing tenant appeal as business activity shifts elsewhere.
Tenants moving from older buildings to newer, better-specified ones.
A rise in the cap rate buyers demand, lowering value even with unchanged rent.

points: A single commercial tenant exit can cost well over a year of rent once vacancy, holding costs, rent-free months, brokerage and refurbishment are counted.
Single-tenant units are binary bets; diversification across tenants, sectors, buildings and cities is hard to achieve through direct ownership.
Functional obsolescence can be fixed with capital spending; locational obsolescence is largely outside your control.
Strata buildings suffer most from ageing because owners rarely agree to fund upgrades.
Rising cap rates can cut value by more than 10% without any change in rent.
Keep a cash reserve, watch early warning signs, and consider REITs for diversification an individual cannot build alone.

body.text: Rents, costs, vacancy periods and valuations in this lesson are illustrative. Market vacancy levels vary widely by city, micro-market and building grade. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any property or security.
